(2) "Delete the AddScheduleCalendar … the calendar contributes nothing" is wrong about the code path. `RecurringTask.ValidateExclusions` nulls an empty exclusion set (RecurringTask.cs:232-235 via `ScheduleExclusionNormalizer.Normalize`), and `ScheduleEvaluator.NormalizeCursorAsync` short-circuits on `Exclusions is null` returning the cursor verbatim (ScheduleEvaluator.cs:83-84) — under the proposed rewrite the assertions hold only because `FirstOccurrenceOnOrAfter` is never reached. REFUTED — the code does exactly what the cited invariant says, and the cost model the finding attacks is the one the spec deliberately chose and bounded.

1) The invariant is satisfied as written, not violated. Spec §5.2 (review/recurring-exclusion-calendars-spec.md:196-204): "At each **top-level evaluator call**, `ScheduleEvaluator` builds an internal evaluation clone... resolution is one dictionary hit per name plus a bounded merge, per top-level evaluator call — **not per door probe**." A "door probe" is a specific term of art in this codebase: the candidate iterations inside `RecurringTask.FilterExcludedCandidates` (RecurringTask.cs:641-655, budget `MaxExclusionSearchIterations` = 200k). `ScheduleEvaluator.NextAfterAsync` IS a top-level evaluator call; resolving once at its entry (ScheduleEvaluator.cs:41) is literally the specified behaviour. The finding silently rewrites "top-level evaluator call" into "PASS (plan/advance)" and then reports the difference as a breach. The spec never says that, and §5.2 goes further: it explicitly rules OUT the cross-call cache the finding implicitly demands ("no reference-keyed cache to leak or serve stale entries — `RecurringTask` and its arrays are mutable persisted objects; a cross-call cache keyed on them is unsafe by construction").

2) The existing guard that makes the cost flat is the cap the spec names. `ScheduleExclusionNormalizer.MaxEntries = 1000` bounds Dates+Ranges of the RESOLVED union *combined* (ScheduleExclusionNormalizer.cs:12, 87-92), `MaxCalendars = 16` bounds the lookups pre-merge. So one `Resolve` is hard-bounded at ≤1000 sorted entries and ≤1000 range allocations, whatever the host registers — exactly the "the union cap makes that cost flat" argument. The finding's "up to 1000 dates + 1000 ranges" doubles the real cap, and "allocates ~1000 `ExclusionRange` objects" per resolve is wrong by an order of magnitude in its own scenario: the `Ranges.Select(new ExclusionRange...)` allocates one per calendar RANGE (~100 in its scenario), not one per union entry. Its ~6.3e5-allocation headline is ~10x inflated.

3) The "orders of magnitude vs inline" claim collapses against the door's own cost. `TryGetExclusionRegionExit` (RecurringTask.cs:719-745) evaluates each candidate with `exclusions.Dates.Contains(localDate)` — a LINEAR array scan — plus a full linear pass over `exclusions.Ranges`. So a single door probe is already O(union) with the same tiny constants; the per-call merge is O(union log union), i.e. a small constant multiple of the probes each call performs anyway. An inline-exclusion schedule with the same 1000 entries pays the same per-probe scans; the calendar delta is a bounded constant per evaluator call, not an order of magnitude on the path.

4) The scenario's arithmetic does not survive the code. (a) The "up to 500 more for the already-served walk" term requires slots that ALREADY have occurrence rows — a host returning from a three-week outage materialized nothing, so `served` stays 0 and that branch never runs (the walk exists for a rewound cursor / externally written rows, OccurrenceMaterializer.cs:512-544). (b) Even when it does run, every one of those iterations already performs `BuildOccurrenceAsync` (payload serialization) + `storage.MaterializeOccurrence` + `storage.TryAdvanceScheduleCursor` — two DB round trips per iteration (OccurrenceMaterializer.cs:497-537). A ≤1000-entry in-memory merge is noise next to that, and `MaxServedSlotsPerRun = 500` is itself the guard bounding the pass. (c) The "~129 for the SkipOldest bisection" requires `eligible.Count > maxOccurrences` (DueSlotEnumerator.cs:326); the scenario states maxOccurrences: 500 against a 21-slot daily backlog, so `FindNthSlotFromEndAsync` is never reached on that path at all. The ~635 figure is roughly 5 in the scenario as described.

5) The sub-claim about `ResolveCalendars` sitting before the `cap == 0` early-out (ScheduleEvaluator.cs:102 vs 106) is textually true but unreachable in production: the ONLY caller is DueSlotEnumerator.cs:381, guarded by `take == 0 ? Array.Empty<DateTimeOffset>() : await evaluator.EnumerateDueSlotsAsync(...)`, so cap is never 0 there.

What survives is a legitimate, low-priority micro-optimization note, not a defect against the stated invariant: the planner and the materializer could thread the already-resolved clone (whose `Calendars` is emptied, so `ResolveCalendars` self-short-circuits at ScheduleEvaluator.cs:136) down through `NextSlotAfterAsync` / the bisection instead of re-resolving per grid step. That is a signature change across `IScheduleEvaluator`'s callers and a design choice the spec deliberately did not make in v1 — it is not the invariant breach, correctness bug, or "orders of magnitude" regression the finding reports.

The mechanism is partly real but the finding's invariant claim, repro and magnitudes all fail.

(1) INVARIANT NOT VIOLATED. Spec §5.2 says resolution is "per top-level evaluator call — not per door probe". A door probe is a candidate inside GetNextOccurrence's anchored filter loop (budget 200,000, ExclusionSearchBudgetExceededException). The code resolves exactly once per public evaluator method and the door probes the already-flattened union. The finding silently redefines "top-level evaluator call" as "pass" and then reports the code for violating its own rewrite.

(2) THE SCENARIO DOES NOT REPRODUCE. With .CatchUp(maxAge: 30d, maxOccurrences: 500).SkipOldest() and a three-week outage of a daily schedule, ~21 slots are owed. PlanCatchUpAsync enters the SkipOldest branch only under `if (eligible.Count > maxOccurrences)` (DueSlotEnumerator.cs:325/345) — 21 > 500 is false, so FindNthSlotFromEndAsync is never invoked; the claimed "~129 resolves for the bisection" is zero in the finding's own repro. The age-window block (lines 272-300) is also skipped since a 3-week-old cursor is newer than a 30-day cutoff. Real count for that run: NormalizeCursorAsync + one CountMissedAsync + EnumerateDueSlotsAsync + one/two successor calls ≈ 5-8 resolves, not ~635.

(3) THE 500-STEP MATERIALIZER WALK NEEDS 500 PRE-EXISTING OCCURRENCES. In MaterializeAsync (OccurrenceMaterializer.cs:472-497) the evaluator call at line 496 is in the `else` arm, reached essentially only on the `!planned` walk — slots that returned AlreadyExists (line 512, served++). A host returning from an outage has none, so served == 0 and the loop makes zero evaluator calls. Planned iterations use plan.Slots[i+1] / plan.NextCursorUtc. Where the served walk can reach 500 (rewound cursor over an already-materialized episode), every iteration also performs storage.MaterializeOccurrence (line 505) — a DB round trip — so ~50-100 µs of in-memory merge per iteration is a fraction of a percent of the loop cost.

(4) BISECTION COST OVERSTATED. MaxBisectionSteps = 64 is documented as a spin guard ("unreachable for any representable range", lines 40-44) and the loop breaks at the first probe counting exactly n (line 728); over a three-week span with a one-day-wide equality region that is ~5 steps, not 64.

(5) PROVIDER GRIDS RESOLVE NOTHING. ResolveCalendars returns immediately on definition.Provider != null (line 136), so the genuinely long loops that are provider-only — WalkForwardAsync's up-to-10,000-step walk (line 645), the memoized bisection chain — cost zero resolutions. TryTakeReading/RememberBacklog are provider-gated (line 616).

(6) ALLOCATION ARITHMETIC INFLATED ~10x. Dates is DateOnly[] (struct); only Ranges allocate. The scenario's ~100 windows give ~200 ExclusionRange allocations per resolve (registry Select + Normalize's rebuild), not ~1000. The 6.3e5 allocations / 1.3e7 comparisons figure multiplies an inflated per-resolve cost by an unreachable resolve count.

(7) The ResolveCalendars-before-early-out observation (line 102 vs 106) is factually correct but not a defect: resolving unconditionally is what keeps "an unresolved definition never evaluates as no exclusions" uniform, and it costs microseconds once per plan.

The highest-volume path — the cap-many due-slot walk — is already resolved once (line 102) and re-enters the short-circuit because the resolved clone's Calendars is empty. What remains is a handful of redundant merges per pass: a legitimate future optimisation, not a violated invariant and not a constructible failing sequence.

REFUTED on two independent grounds — an existing guard makes the stated scenario unreachable, and the parity baseline the finding asserts ("tranche 1 allocated nothing") is factually wrong.

1) The guard: `ScheduleExclusionNormalizer.Normalize` is unreachable for a schedule with no exclusions.
`RecurringTask.Validate` reaches the normalizer only through `ValidateExclusions` (E:/Archivio/Sviluppo/Web/EverTask/src/EverTask/Scheduler/Recurring/RecurringTask.cs:221-240), which opens with

    if (Exclusions is not { } exclusions)
        return;

`ScheduleExclusionNormalizer.Normalize(exclusions)` is at line 232, strictly after that early return. `Exclusions` is a nullable property (`public ScheduleExclusions? Exclusions { get; set; }`, RecurringTask.cs:23) that defaults to null and is additionally re-nulled whenever normalization collapses to empty (line 234). Grep confirms RecurringTask.cs:232 is the ONLY Validate-path caller of `Normalize`; the other two callers (ScheduleCalendarRegistry.cs:23,49 and EverTaskServiceConfiguration.cs:517) are the calendar-resolution and startup-registration paths, which by definition only run for definitions that name calendars, or once at AddEverTask.

This kills the finding's headline scenario outright. In the "200k-row recovery backlog" case, the rows are pre-existing schedules with no exclusions at all — `RecurringTask` deserializes with `Exclusions == null`, `ValidateExclusions` returns at line 230, and the normalizer allocates exactly zero. `RecoveredTaskFactory.FromRow` (RecoveredTaskFactory.cs:93) and both recovery waves therefore pay nothing from the cited code. The finding conflates "no calendars" with "reaches Normalize"; only rows that carry inline exclusions reach it at all, and those are a small, opt-in minority (the feature is new).

2) The baseline: for the rows that DO reach it, tranche 1 was not allocation-free either. `git show 5579959:.../RecurringTask.cs` lines 240-241 already ran, unconditionally and without any empty-input guard, the exact same pattern twice:

    exclusions.Days  = exclusions.Days.Distinct().Order().ToArray();
    exclusions.Dates = exclusions.Dates.Distinct().Order().ToArray();

plus `new List<ExclusionRange>(...)` twice (lines 243, 270) and `merged.ToArray()` (283) — on a row whose `Days`/`Dates`/`Ranges` may all be empty. So the pre-move body already spent roughly a dozen short-lived gen0 objects per call for a possibly-empty input. `NormalizeCalendarNames` adds a third instance of a pattern the method already used twice: one 24-byte `new string[0]`, a Distinct iterator, an OrderedEnumerable and its enumerators (`ToArray()` over an empty sequence returns `Array.Empty<string>()`, so no fourth array). That is roughly +30% on an already-allocating validator that runs once per dispatch or once per recovered exclusion-bearing row — not "where tranche 1 allocated nothing", and not a new per-call cost class.

3) Behavioural parity — the invariant actually stated — holds. For a no-calendar definition `NormalizeCalendarNames([])` returns an empty array, the collapse condition at lines 75-78 adds `Calendars.Length == 0` to the three tranche-1 terms and so evaluates identically, and `Exclusions = null` is still assigned. Evaluation and validation are byte-identical in outcome; only a handful of transient bytes differ.

4) Call-site frequency confirms the severity is misjudged even in the reachable case. Grep shows exactly three `Validate(` schedule call sites (Dispatcher.cs:409, TaskScheduleManager.cs:368, RecoveredTaskFactory.cs:93) — once per dispatch, once per runtime schedule change, once per recovered row. None sits in a per-occurrence or per-slot loop; the hot exclusion path is `GetNextOccurrence`, which the normalizer is not on. And each of those three sites already allocates a `new ScheduleValidationContext(...)` (an internal sealed *record*, i.e. a class) per call, on every row including the no-exclusion 200k ones — an allocation that happens before the guard and dwarfs, in reachability terms, the one being reported. The cited line is not where any measurable per-call cost lives.

Net: the causal chain's key link ("Validate() → ValidateExclusions → Normalize" for a calendar-free row) is severed by an explicit null guard; the parity claim rests on a misreading of the pre-move body, which allocated the same way. Not a defect.

ledger.title: Row-rebuild validation is only tested on the recovery path — the repark hole the spec names by hand is unpinned
ledger.invariant: calendars-spec §4.3 and §7: "Row-rebuild validation: each §4.3 path (recovery, schedule retry, materializer, repark) refuses/poisons an unknown name instead of executing once." §4.3 singles out `WorkerExecutor.ReparkFromRowAsync` as "the last one [that] today deserializes without validating and parks the stored cursor directly, which would let a row naming an unknown calendar execute once before any evaluator lookup throws."
ledger.causal_chain: The four §4.3 rebuild paths were all converted to `ScheduleValidationContext`: `WorkerService` recovery (WorkerService.cs:253, :345), `RetryScheduleDecisionAsync` (WorkerExecutor.cs:474), the materializer's run and repark builder (OccurrenceMaterializer.cs:223, :698), and `ReparkFromRowAsync` (WorkerExecutor.cs:2011). Only the recovery path has a test that exercises an UNKNOWN calendar: `WorkerServiceRecoveryPoisonTests.Should_poison_a_recovered_schedule_that_names_an_unregistered_calendar` and `...when_a_calendar_edit_makes_its_resolved_union_invalid`. No test in the tranche drives `ReparkFromRowAsync`, `RetryScheduleDecisionAsync` or `OccurrenceMaterializer` with a row whose `Calendars` name something the registry does not hold. The repark case is exactly the regression the tranche was written to close, and it is the one whose failure mode is a real EXECUTION (an inline recurring row parked at its stored cursor runs the handler at that slot before anything asks the evaluator).
ledger.failure_scenario: Revert the two edits at WorkerExecutor.cs:2010-2011 back to `var recovered = RecoveredTaskFactory.FromRow(row);` (no context) and move the scope creation back below the null guard. Every test in this tranche still passes: `ReparkFromRowAsync` then rebuilds a row naming "removed-holidays", `scheduler.TrySchedule(executor, cursor)` succeeds, and the schedule fires its stored cursor once with the calendar's exclusions silently absent — a host that lost its holiday config runs the holiday slot. The `ArgumentException` only appears afterwards, on the next advance, by which time the run has happened. The same revert on `RetryScheduleDecisionAsync` (WorkerExecutor.cs:474) and on the materializer (OccurrenceMaterializer.cs:223, :698) is likewise invisible to the suite.
ledger.evidence: Guarded code: src/EverTask/Worker/WorkerExecutor.cs:2010-2017 (scope moved above `FromRow`, context passed, null-`Recurring` logged via `ScheduleReparkFromRowFailed`). Sole unknown-name rebuild tests: test/EverTask.Tests/WorkerServiceRecoveryPoisonTests.cs:91-163 (recovery only) and test/EverTask.Tests/RecoveredTaskFactoryTests.cs:197-217 (the factory in isolation, not a caller). `rg -l "ExceptCalendar|Calendars = \[" test/` returns no file touching the repark, schedule-retry or materializer rebuild with an unregistered name.
ledger.fix_sketch: Add three tests over the shared `MemoryTaskStorage` pattern the reschedule/durable suites already use: (1) seed an inline recurring row whose JSON names an unregistered calendar, drive a lost-CAS advance so `ReparkFromRowAsync` runs, and assert the row is NOT registered with the scheduler and `ScheduleReparkFromRowFailed` is logged with the calendar name; (2) arm an `IsScheduleRetry` delivery over such a row and assert `RetryScheduleDecisionAsync` refuses instead of re-deciding; (3) call `OccurrenceMaterializer.RunAsync` on a durable row naming an unregistered calendar and assert it parks the row as unusable rather than materializing a slot.
